notes.definition: The heart is an organ that pumps blood around the body in a double circulatory system. Blood travels through three types of blood vessel (arteries, veins and capillaries), and the lungs are adapted for exchanging oxygen and carbon dioxide with the blood.
explanation: Humans have a double circulatory system: blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit of the body. The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs, where gas exchange happens. Oxygenated blood returns to the heart and the left ventricle pumps it around the rest of the body. Pumping blood back to the heart before sending it to the body keeps the pressure high, so oxygen is delivered quickly to respiring cells.

The heart has four chambers. The atria (top) receive blood and the ventricles (bottom) pump it out. Deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium from the vena cava, passes to the right ventricle and leaves through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns in the pulmonary vein to the left atrium, passes to the left ventricle and leaves in the aorta. The left ventricle wall is thicker because it pumps blood around the whole body. Valves prevent backflow. The heart muscle receives its own oxygen supply from the coronary arteries.

The natural resting heart rate is controlled by a group of cells in the right atrium that act as a pacemaker, sending electrical impulses that make the heart muscle contract. If this goes wrong, an artificial pacemaker, a small electrical device fitted under the skin, can be used to correct irregularities in the heart rate.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure. They have thick walls of muscle and elastic fibres, which stretch and recoil with each heartbeat, and a narrow lumen. Veins carry blood back to the heart at low pressure. They have thinner walls, a large lumen and valves to stop blood flowing backwards. Capillaries connect arteries and veins. Their walls are one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance so substances such as oxygen and glucose can be exchanged with body cells.

Air enters the lungs through the trachea, which divides into two bronchi, then into smaller bronchioles ending in tiny air sacs called alveoli. Alveoli are adapted for gas exchange: there are millions of them, giving a very large surface area; their walls are one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance; and each is surrounded by a network of capillaries, keeping a steep concentration gradient. Oxygen diffuses from the air into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the air.

Rate of blood flow is a simple compound measure: rate = volume of blood ÷ time. For example, if 300 cm³ of blood passes through an artery in 60 s, the rate is 5 cm³/s. Make sure you convert units (minutes to seconds, cm³ to dm³) where needed.
keyFacts: Double circulation: right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs; left ventricle pumps blood to the rest of the body.
Vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta.
The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall than the right ventricle.
Coronary arteries supply oxygenated blood to the heart muscle.
The natural pacemaker is a group of cells in the right atrium.
Artificial pacemakers are electrical devices that correct an irregular heart rate.
Arteries: thick muscular and elastic walls, high pressure. Veins: thin walls, large lumen, valves. Capillaries: walls one cell thick.
Alveoli have a large surface area, thin walls and a rich blood supply.
Rate of blood flow = volume of blood ÷ time.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all arteries carry oxygenated blood and all veins carry deoxygenated blood.
misconceptions.right: In fact the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood. Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry blood towards it.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the left side of the heart is on the left of a diagram.
misconceptions.right: In fact heart diagrams are drawn as if you are facing the person, so the left side of the heart appears on the right of the page.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the heart gets oxygen from the blood inside its chambers.
misconceptions.right: In fact the heart muscle is supplied by the coronary arteries, which branch from the aorta.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think veins have valves because blood is under high pressure.
misconceptions.right: In fact veins have valves because blood is under low pressure, and the valves stop it flowing backwards.

realWorld: Artificial pacemakers are fitted to hundreds of thousands of people each year to treat slow or irregular heartbeats.
Doctors measure pulse rate in arteries at the wrist or neck because arteries have a pulse caused by the stretching and recoiling of their elastic walls.
Blood samples are taken from veins rather than arteries because veins are near the surface and blood in them is at low pressure.
examTips: Remember the order of blood flow by starting at the vena cava and following through to the aorta; write it out as a chain.
Explain the thicker left ventricle wall by linking it to pumping blood at higher pressure around the whole body, not just 'pumping harder'.
When explaining vessel structure, always link each feature to its function (for example 'one cell thick so short diffusion distance').
In rate of blood flow calculations, check units: convert minutes to seconds if the answer is per second.
For alveoli, give three adaptations: large surface area, thin walls, good blood supply (concentration gradient).
summary: The heart pumps blood in a double circulation: to the lungs and to the body.
Right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs; left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body.
The pacemaker in the right atrium controls resting heart rate; artificial pacemakers correct irregularities.
Arteries, veins and capillaries have structures matched to pressure and exchange.
Alveoli have a large surface area, thin walls and rich blood supply for gas exchange.
Rate of blood flow = volume ÷ time.

questions.explanation: D is the left ventricle (the left side of the heart is shown on the right of the diagram). It pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta. C, the right ventricle, pumps blood to the lungs; the atria (A and B) pump blood only into the ventricles.

questions.question: Which blood vessel carries blood away from the heart to the body?
questions.explanation: The aorta leaves the left ventricle. The vena cava and pulmonary vein bring blood to the heart.

questions.question: Which type of blood vessel has walls only one cell thick?
questions.explanation: Capillaries have very thin walls so substances can diffuse in and out quickly.

questions.question: Where is the group of cells that controls the natural resting heart rate?
questions.explanation: The pacemaker cells are in the wall of the right atrium.

questions.question: Which vessel carries deoxygenated blood?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. It is the exception to 'arteries carry oxygenated blood'.

questions.question: What is the function of the coronary arteries?
options: To carry blood from the heart to the lungs
To supply the heart muscle with oxygenated blood
To return blood from the heart muscle to the right atrium
To carry blood from the lungs to the left atrium
questions.explanation: Heart muscle needs its own blood supply for respiration, delivered by the coronary arteries.

questions.question: Which feature helps veins return blood to the heart?
questions.explanation: Valves stop low-pressure blood flowing backwards. Thick elastic walls are an artery feature.

questions.question: What is the correct path of blood through the right side of the heart?
options: Vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery
Pulmonary vein → right atrium → right ventricle → aorta
Vena cava → right ventricle → right atrium → pulmonary artery
Aorta → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary vein
questions.explanation: Blood from the body enters the right atrium, passes into the right ventricle and is pumped into the pulmonary artery.

questions.question: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than the wall of the right ventricle?
options: It pumps a larger volume of blood than the right ventricle each beat
It must generate higher pressure to pump blood around the whole body
It receives blood at higher pressure from the lungs
questions.explanation: Both ventricles pump the same volume per beat. The left needs more muscle to produce higher pressure to push blood around the whole body, whereas the lungs are close by.

questions.question:
Humans have a double circulatory system.
Which statement best explains an advantage of a double circulatory system?
options: Blood only needs to pass through the heart once
Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix, which increases oxygen delivery
Blood is returned to the heart after the lungs and pumped again at high pressure, so oxygen reaches tissues quickly
It means arteries do not need elastic walls
questions.explanation: Blood loses pressure passing through the lung capillaries. Returning to the heart lets the left ventricle re-pressurise it for efficient delivery to the body.

questions.question: Where in the lungs does gas exchange take place?
questions.explanation: Gas exchange happens across the thin walls of the alveoli; the other structures are airways.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the volume of blood that flowed through an artery in 40 seconds.
Calculate the rate of blood flow through the artery.
Use the equation:
rate of blood flow = volume of blood ÷ time
questions.explanation: rate = volume ÷ time = 600 ÷ 40 = 15 cm³/s.

questions.question:
A student counts 21 pulse beats in 15 seconds.
Calculate the student's heart rate in beats per minute.
questions.explanation: 60 ÷ 15 = 4, so 21 × 4 = 84 beats per minute.

questions.question:
Blood flows through a vein at a rate of 4.5 cm³/s.
Calculate the volume of blood that flows through the vein in 3 minutes.
questions.explanation: volume = rate × time. Convert the time to seconds first: 4.5 × 180 = 810 cm³.

questions.question:

Calculate the rate of blood flow out of the left ventricle.
Give your answer in dm³ per minute.

headers: Volume of blood pumped by the left ventricle per beat in cm³
Heart rate in beats per minute

questions.explanation: Volume per minute = 70 × 72 = 5040 cm³. Since 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³, this is 5.04 dm³/min.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the rate of blood flow to a muscle at rest and during exercise.
Calculate the percentage increase in the rate of blood flow to the muscle during exercise.

headers: Rate of blood flow to the muscle in cm³/s

questions.explanation: Increase = 11.2 cm³/s. 11.2 ÷ 0.8 = 14, × 100 = 1400%. Dividing 12 by 0.8 gives 15 times the original, which is a 1400% increase, not 1500%.

questions.question: Give the function of the valves in the heart.
markScheme: 1 mark: to prevent blood flowing backwards (backflow)
questions.explanation: Valves ensure blood flows in one direction through the heart.

1 mark: Q is the pulmonary artery
questions.explanation: Deoxygenated blood from the body enters via the vena cava and leaves for the lungs via the pulmonary artery.

questions.question: Explain why a person with a faulty natural pacemaker might be fitted with an artificial pacemaker.
markScheme: 1 mark: the natural pacemaker (in the right atrium) controls resting heart rate, so a fault causes an irregular / too slow heart rate
1 mark: an artificial pacemaker is an electrical device that sends impulses to correct the heart rate
questions.explanation: If the heart rate is irregular, organs may not receive enough oxygenated blood; the artificial device restores a regular rhythm.

questions.question: Explain how the structure of an artery is related to its function.
markScheme: 1 mark: arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure
1 mark: thick muscular wall withstands high pressure
1 mark: elastic fibres allow the wall to stretch and recoil, smoothing blood flow / maintaining pressure
questions.explanation: Each structural feature must be linked to the high-pressure blood the artery carries.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows an alveolus and a blood capillary in the lungs.
Describe three ways the alveoli are adapted for efficient gas exchange.

markScheme: 1 mark: millions of alveoli give a large surface area
1 mark: walls one cell thick give a short diffusion distance
1 mark: rich network of capillaries maintains a steep concentration gradient
questions.explanation: These three features all increase the rate of diffusion of oxygen into, and carbon dioxide out of, the blood.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows cross-sections of an artery and a vein.
Compare the structure of arteries and veins.
Explain the differences.

figure.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 230" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="110" cy="110" r="70" fill="#fca5a5" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="110" cy="110" r="52" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><circle cx="110" cy="110" r="22" fill="#e5e7eb" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor"/><path d="M265 60Q330 40 385 65Q410 110 385 160Q320 185 265 160Q240 110 265 60Z" fill="#93c5fd" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><path d="M273 70Q330 52 377 73Q399 110 377 152Q320 173 273 151Q252 110 273 70Z" fill="#e5e7eb" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="currentColor"/><text x="110" y="205" font-size="14" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">Artery</text><text x="325" y="205" font-size="14" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">Vein</text><line x1="110" y1="110" x2="64" y2="20" stroke="currentColor"/><text x="60" y="24" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">Lumen</text><line x1="150" y1="60" x2="190" y2="20" stroke="currentColor"/><text x="194" y="24" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start">Wall</text><text x="325" y="114" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">Lumen</text><line x1="392" y1="95" x2="398" y2="30" stroke="currentColor"/><text x="402" y="34" font-size="12" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start">Wall</text></svg>

markScheme: 1 mark: arteries have thicker, more muscular and elastic walls than veins, because blood in arteries is at high pressure
1 mark: veins have a larger lumen, reducing resistance to low-pressure blood flow
1 mark: veins have valves to prevent backflow, arteries do not (except at the heart)
questions.explanation: A comparison needs both vessels in each point. Linking every difference to pressure gains the explanation marks.

questions.question:
The lumen of a capillary is only just wide enough for red blood cells to pass through one at a time.
Suggest how this helps the exchange of oxygen with body cells.
acceptedAnswers: red blood cells close to wall
markScheme: 1 mark: red blood cells are pressed close to the capillary wall, so the diffusion distance is short
1 mark: blood flows slowly, giving more time for diffusion
questions.explanation: A narrow lumen reduces the distance oxygen must travel from haemoglobin to tissue cells and slows flow, both increasing exchange.

questions.question: Name the tube that carries air from the mouth and nose towards the lungs.
questions.explanation: The trachea divides into the bronchi, which lead into each lung.

questions.question:
Blood flows through a capillary bed at a rate of 0.05 cm³/s.
What volume of blood passes through the capillary bed in one hour?
questions.explanation: One hour = 3600 s, and 0.05 × 3600 = 180 cm³. Option A uses 60 s instead of 3600 s.

questions.question: Describe the pathway taken by blood from the vena cava to the aorta, naming the chambers, vessels and organ it passes through.
markScheme: Indicative content: deoxygenated blood enters right atrium from vena cava; passes through valve into right ventricle; right ventricle pumps it into pulmonary artery; to the lungs where it picks up oxygen and loses carbon dioxide; returns as oxygenated blood in pulmonary vein; enters left atrium; passes through valve into left ventricle; left ventricle pumps it into aorta to the body.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): the full sequence in the correct order with correct vessel and chamber names, mentioning the lungs and the change in oxygenation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some chambers or vessels named in a partly correct order.
questions.explanation: A clear numbered sequence is the easiest way to show the full order. Do not swap the pulmonary artery and vein.

questions.question: Explain how the heart, blood vessels and lungs work together to supply oxygen to respiring muscle cells. Include how the structure of each part is adapted to its function.
markScheme: Indicative content: double circulation: right ventricle pumps blood to lungs, left ventricle to body; left ventricle has thicker muscular wall to generate high pressure; valves prevent backflow; pacemaker in right atrium sets the rate; lungs: trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli; alveoli have large surface area, thin walls, rich capillary supply; oxygen diffuses into blood down a concentration gradient; ventilation maintains gradient; oxygenated blood returns in pulmonary vein; aorta and arteries carry it at high pressure with thick muscular elastic walls; capillaries have walls one cell thick so oxygen diffuses into muscle cells; deoxygenated blood returns in veins (valves, large lumen) to vena cava.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): coherent explanation linking heart, lungs and vessels, with structure explicitly linked to function for each.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes the route of oxygen with some structure and function links.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about the heart, lungs or vessels with little linking.
questions.explanation: The best answers follow an oxygen molecule from the alveolus to the muscle cell and justify each structure on the way.

questions.question:
A pulse can be felt in arteries but not in veins.
What is the main reason for this?
options: Veins are deeper in the body than all arteries
Arteries have elastic walls that stretch and recoil as high-pressure blood surges through after each heartbeat
Veins contain valves that block the pulse
questions.explanation: The pulse is the stretch and recoil of the artery wall with each beat. By the time blood reaches veins the pressure is low and steady.
